reports.title: Government of Thailand and Chaiwat Limlikhitaksorn v. Wuth Boonlert and Samak Donnapee
reports.status_label: Acquittal upheld on appeal; later separate defamation case involving Wuth settled
reports.status_qualification: The latest verified decision in the original Chaiwat prosecution is the Court of Appeal's 22 December 2020 acquittal. The 26 September 2023 event concerns a distinct case involving Wuth and another defendant, not Samak. No Supreme Court disposition or certificate of finality in the original proceedings was verified.
executive: Thailand's response to UN special procedures confirms that the Court of Appeal upheld both acquittals on 22 December 2020. The prosecutor did not appeal; private co-plaintiff Chaiwat did. [S1]
The latest dated personal follow-up is a separate defamation settlement involving Wuth and Suracha Boonyeim on 26 September 2023, documented by CFJ in September 2024. It does not concern Samak. [S3]
baseline: The supplied July 2020 report concerns a criminal-defamation prosecution arising from Facebook commentary about alleged land-related misconduct by an official. Samak was accused of publishing the posts, while Wuth was accused of sharing them without adding commentary. The allegedly defamatory passages did not expressly name Chaiwat. The charge was brought under section 328 of Thailand's Criminal Code, and the proceedings also exposed the defendants to a private compensation claim. Both defendants were human-rights defenders whose work addressed Karen communities and land rights. [O]

TrialWatch monitored hearings between September and November 2019. On 18 November 2019, the trial court acquitted both defendants of all charges and rejected the co-plaintiff's compensation demand. The report nevertheless distinguished an acquittal from a prosecution free of rights concerns: the defendants had already borne the burdens of criminal proceedings over public-interest speech. [O]

Lionel Blackman, the report's TrialWatch expert, assigned the original grade C. The assessment described generally fair trial procedures but questioned the prosecution and acceptance of a weak criminal-defamation case against activists. Its concern was not that the defendants had received prison sentences; they had been acquitted. Rather, the report addressed the potential chilling effect and misuse of criminal process. This follow-up retains that historical attribution and assigns no new grade. [O]

timeline.event: Trial court acquitted Wuth and Samak and rejected compensation in the original case.
CFJ published its statement accompanying the TrialWatch assessment.
Court of Appeal upheld the original acquittal, according to Thailand's response to UN special procedures.
Separate Surapon Naknakorn defamation case against Wuth and Suracha Boonyeim settled.

developments: The government's account describes the appellate court's acceptance of good-faith public criticism. This is a government response hosted by UNESCO, not the judgment itself. Although its title names an April 2020 UN communication, its contents extend into 2021; its precise publication date is unstated. [S1]

The separate case documented in CFJ's 2024 report concerned 2014 posts criticizing Thairath reporter Surapon Naknakorn's alleged conflict of interest. A complaint followed in September 2020 and an indictment in September 2022. The 2023 settlement provided for withdrawal of civil and criminal claims in exchange for an apology, publication of that apology, and 100,000 baht compensation. CFJ reports that the defendants accepted because they no longer wished to continue going to court. Different speech, complainant, and co-defendant establish that this was another proceeding. [S3]
analysis: Analytical inference: appellate affirmation is significant, but the available account does not establish every subsequent procedural step or unappealable finality. [S1]
Analytical inference: the separate settlement concerns litigation burden; it supplies no evidence that Samak was prosecuted again or the original acquittal disturbed. [S3]
conclusion: Appellate acquittal is verified; subsequent finality needs documentation. The separate settlement changes neither original defendant's documented trial outcome. [S1] [S3]
gaps: Obtain the 22 December 2020 appellate judgment and any record of a Supreme Court petition or certificate of finality.
Confirm whether either original defendant obtained compensation or another remedy for the costs of this prosecution.
Obtain a current, case-specific account from counsel or the defendants; the 2023 settlement does not establish either person's circumstances in October 2026.

reports.title: Kazakhstan v. Alnur Ilyashev
reports.status_label: Original restrictions reportedly completed in part; UN remedy outstanding; separate 2026 investigation
reports.status_qualification: Freedom Now explicitly reports release from house arrest on 17 April 2023. A 30 April 2025 interview says the five-year public-activity ban was due to expire later that year, not that expiry had already been formally confirmed. September 2026 reporting describes release after questioning in a separate fraud investigation as a witness with a right to defence and an undertaking to appear. No current custodial order or domestic reversal of the 2020 conviction was verified.
executive: The latest verified personal event is Ilyashev's questioning after a home search on 4 September 2026 in a separate fraud investigation. Azattyq reported on 18 September that he was released with an undertaking to appear and had witness-with-right-to-defence status. Adil Soz's monitoring, published 8 October, also records his return home. These accounts do not establish a new conviction or a retrial of the original speech case. [S4] [S5]

Earlier follow-up includes an express report of release on 17 April 2023 and a UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention finding against Kazakhstan in March 2022. Neither establishes that the original conviction was expunged or the requested reparations provided. [S1] [S2]
baseline: The supplied March 2021 report concerns Facebook criticism of the ruling Nur Otan party and the government's COVID-19 response. Ilyashev was arrested on 17 April 2020 and prosecuted under Article 274 for allegedly spreading false information during a state of emergency. The monitored trial took place in June 2020 by videoconference, with repeated connection failures and concerns about confidential access to counsel and the effective examination of witnesses and expert evidence. [O]

On 22 June 2020 the court imposed three years of restricted liberty, compulsory labor, and a five-year prohibition on civic or public activities. Restricted liberty was not an acquittal or an unconditional release. The Almaty City Court upheld the conviction on 15 September 2020; the original report also records unsuccessful Supreme Court review. The content and reach of the additional activity ban were central concerns because it potentially restricted protected expression and association beyond the movement-related sentence. [O]

TrialWatch expert Vania Costa Ramos assigned the original grade D. Her assessment addressed fairness defects and the disproportionate prosecution of political criticism. The historical grade is attributed to that report only. No later development is used here to calculate a replacement TrialWatch score. [O]

timeline.event: Convicted; three-year restriction-of-liberty sentence and five-year civic/public-activity ban imposed.

developments: The Working Group classified the deprivation of liberty as arbitrary under categories I, II, III and V. It requested quashing the sentence, expunging the criminal record, compensation and other reparations, and an independent investigation. This is a verified international finding, not evidence that Kazakhstan implemented those measures. [S1]

Freedom Now's case page expressly dates release, avoiding an inference from the nominal sentence length. In his April 2025 Vlast interview, Ilyashev described renewed work as a consultant but continuing inability to join the legal-consultants chamber because of his criminal record. He said the public/political ban would expire that year; the interview does not itself certify its eventual termination. [S2] [S3]
TrialWatch's 2025 submission identifies a separate Human Rights Committee communication as submitted but awaiting registration. No later Committee disposition was verified. [S6]

The 2026 investigation was reported as fraud-related, not an Article 274 speech prosecution. The most reliable accessible accounts identify witness status rather than a proven offence. The October monitoring's publication date should not be mistaken for a new October detention. [S5]
analysis: Analytical inference: completion of movement restrictions can coexist with unresolved conviction-related consequences. The interview supplies a concrete example through professional exclusion. A UN finding and a reported release therefore answer different questions: the former addresses unlawfulness and remedy; the latter addresses a particular restraint. [S1] [S2] [S3]
Analytical inference: a separate investigation proves neither guilt nor political motivation. Full-text reporting supports release with an undertaking to appear, not house arrest. [S4]
conclusion: The documented trajectory is international condemnation, reported release, and continuing collateral concerns, followed by a distinct 2026 investigation. As of the cutoff, a domestic reversal, expungement, implemented reparations, and the outcome of the new investigation remain unverified. [S1] [S3] [S4]
gaps: Was the original conviction quashed or criminal record expunged following WGAD Opinion No. 2/2022?
Were compensation or other reparations implemented?
Was the five-year activity ban formally terminated, and were professional-registration restrictions removed?
What is the registration number and subsequent status of the separate Human Rights Committee communication?
Did the September 2026 fraud investigation alter Ilyashev's witness status or impose any later restrictions?

reports.title: Russian Federation v. Alexander Pichugin
reports.status_label: ECtHR found freedom-of-expression violation; domestic reversal and payment unverified
reports.status_qualification: The ECtHR's final committee judgment addresses the original speech conviction and a separate protest case. The EUR 10,000 award covers the applicant's combined findings, not exclusively the speech prosecution. A foreign-agent designation on 7 November 2025 is separately reported. No new prison sentence, domestic acquittal, or payment of the Strasbourg award was verified.
executive: On 13 November 2025, the European Court of Human Rights ruled in Pichugin's favor in Vlasov and Others v. Russia. His representing Media Defence Centre explains that the judgment addressed both the COVID-19 satire prosecution and a distinct protest-related case, with EUR 10,000 awarded. This is the latest verified judicial event identified. [S3]

A separate development preceded that judgment: the Justice Ministry added the Nizhny Novgorod journalist to the foreign-agent register on 7 November 2025. That designation is not a terrorism-list entry or another sentence under the provision used in the original report. [S4]
baseline: The supplied April 2022 report concerns journalist Alexander Pichugin, also transliterated Aleksandr, and his Telegram channel Sorokin Khvost. It is not the case of imprisoned former Yukos employee Alexey Pichugin. The subject and channel, the 300,000-ruble fine, and counsel's identity provide safeguards against that consequential name confusion. [O]

The prosecution arose from a satirical 12 April 2020 post criticizing church gatherings during the COVID-19 pandemic. Under Article 207.1, authorities treated the commentary as knowingly false information about a public threat. On 11 November 2020, the Bogorodsk City Court convicted Pichugin and imposed a 300,000-ruble fine. It did not impose a custodial sentence. The TrialWatch monitoring covered proceedings from July to November 2020. [O]

TrialWatch expert Oliver Wallasch assigned the historical grade D. The report identified shortcomings in proof of intent, treatment of linguistic evidence and reasoning, including the handling of evidence supporting a metaphorical reading of the post. It also assessed the interference with freedom of expression. Those are the original report's findings, not a fresh grading exercise or a claim that later courts adopted every TrialWatch criticism. [O]

timeline.event: Bogorodsk City Court convicted Pichugin and imposed a 300,000-ruble fine.

developments: Contemporaneous reporting confirms that the regional appeal was rejected on 26 January 2021. Counsel Tumas Misakyan then intended to pursue cassation and Strasbourg proceedings. An announced intention alone would not establish filing; the later ECtHR appendix supplies the application number and actual introduction date. [S1] [S2]
The ECtHR found disproportionate interference with Article 10 in the satire prosecution and expressly states that its committee judgment is final. [S2]

The representing lawyers describe separate protest-related findings under Articles 5, 6 and 11, alongside the speech finding. The EUR 10,000 award covers the combined complaints rather than the original prosecution alone. [S3]

The lawyer organization's same-day account independently ties the European decision to the journalist and original post. It explains the combined rights findings and compensation award, reinforcing identification while not proving that the award was paid or that Russian courts removed the conviction. [S3]

Kommersant's November 2025 report connects the foreign-agent designation to the same journalist and the COVID satire conviction. It also reports that he had lived outside Russia since 2022. That is a dated account of relocation, not verification of his residence or legal security on 9 October 2026. The government's allegations associated with designation should not be treated as established facts. [S4]
analysis: Analytical inference: the speech finding supports TrialWatch's expression concern, but does not establish that every original fairness criticism was separately upheld. [O] [S2]

Analytical inference: an international victory and a later designation answer different questions. Neither establishes domestic expungement, payment, present liberty or a new terrorism case. [S2] [S4]
conclusion: The final ECtHR judgment is the strongest verified update. Domestic implementation remains unresolved; foreign-agent designation is a distinct event. [S2] [S4]
gaps: Was the Article 207.1 conviction subsequently reopened, quashed, or expunged domestically?
Was the EUR 10,000 ECtHR award paid, and through what mechanism?
Has the 7 November 2025 foreign-agent designation been challenged or removed?
Are there any later case-specific restrictions or proceedings, confirmed by counsel or court documents, through the cutoff?

reports.title: Section 20 of Pakistan's PECA: Partial Invalidation, the 2025 Amendment and 2026 Enforcement
reports.status_label: 2022 partial invalidation; 2025 statutory expansion; enforcement verified in 2026
reports.status_qualification: Latest located court event is Bilal Ghauri's conditional post-arrest bail, reported on 17 September 2026. The 2022 ruling pre-dates and is discussed in the original. It does not establish repeal of all Section 20. No final merits disposition of the 2025 constitutional challenges or definitive appellate treatment of the 2022 ruling was verified.
executive: This legal-reform follow-up must distinguish the 8 April 2022 judgment already covered by the September 2023 original from actual later change. The Islamabad High Court invalidated the 2022 amendment ordinance and the reputation-harm part of Section 20, not every component of that section. Parliament then enacted a different amendment in January 2025, adding Section 26A and changing enforcement arrangements. [O] [S1] [S2]

The latest verified court event located is Bilal Ghauri's 16 September 2026 bail in a case invoking Sections 20 and 26A. A July 2026 order concerning Asad Toor also addressed disclosure before inquiry. Neither event is an acquittal or a judgment repealing PECA. The original is a reform report without a TrialWatch letter grade. [S5] [S6] [O]
baseline: The original examined notices and proceedings affecting Asad Toor, Absar Alam, Bilal Ghauri and Fawad Ali Shah. It emphasized that the 2016 Section 20 concerned a natural person, not governmental institutions as such, and criticized unclear notices and speech-based investigations. Its recommendations for reform and concessions of unconstitutionality were advocacy conclusions, not themselves changes to the statute. [O]

It already discussed the Islamabad High Court's April 2022 intervention and further constitutional litigation. The follow-up therefore should not present the ordinance's invalidation as a new development after September 2023, or infer a Supreme Court merits judgment from a request for briefing. [O]

timeline.event: IHC invalidates 2022 ordinance and Section 20 to the extent of reputation harm and its punishment; historical baseline event.
Original reform report published; no letter grade.
Act II of 2025 receives assent and commences; new Section 26A and procedural amendments.
Published report of IHC hearing and adjournment of challenges to 6 March; not a merits judgment.
Reported Toor order directs disclosure of allegations before NCCIA inquiry and disposes of his petition.
Ghauri granted conditional post-arrest bail in FIR 143/2026 under Sections 20 and 26A, reported the following day.

developments: The 2022 operative order strikes Section 20 only insofar as it addresses reputational harm and the corresponding punishment. The official consolidated text still prints that phrase alongside intimidation and privacy, so printed consolidation alone does not establish that judicial invalidation was reversed. Its natural-person wording also remains important: a general definition of 'person' cannot silently replace a more specific element. [S1] [S3]

Act II of 2025 creates Section 26A for intentional dissemination of information known, or reasonably believed, to be false or fake and likely to cause public fear, panic, disorder or unrest; the maximum is three years or PKR 2 million, or both. It establishes the NCCIA statutory framework and social-media regulatory machinery. The amended Section 43 places Sections 20 and 26A in the cognizable, non-bailable and non-compoundable category. The Act does not delete Section 20 wholesale. Regulatory content-blocking powers are distinct from that section's criminal elements. [S2] [S3]

The News reported in February 2026 that the IHC was hearing journalists' constitutional challenges and had adjourned them to 6 March. The reported refusal to suspend legislation by interim stay is not a final merits ruling upholding every provision. No later merits disposition of those petitions was verified in this research. [S4]

A July update reports that the IHC ordered the NCCIA to disclose allegations before investigating Toor under Section 26A. Separately, September reporting records Ghauri's bail on PKR 100,000 surety, conditional on his not being required in another case. Bail does not terminate the prosecution; the precise later custody position is not established here. These are new proceedings involving subjects named in the original, not demonstrated dispositions of their original files. [S5] [S6]
analysis: Analytical inference: the authentic statutory text, the operative judicial order and actual enforcement must be read separately. Saying 'Section 20 was repealed' would obscure retained subject matter; saying it operates without qualification would ignore the partial invalidation. An official PDF retaining old wording is not proof of a successful appeal against the court. [S1] [S3]

Analytical inference: post-amendment enforcement illustrates a change in the available charging routes, not proof that their elements were established against any journalist. Notice-specific relief addresses participation in an inquiry, while bail addresses detention. Neither necessarily resolves the constitutional questions or underlying allegations. [S5] [S6]
conclusion: The verified follow-up is selective judicial invalidation followed by fresh legislative expansion and documented 2026 proceedings. The defensible account preserves each provision's scope and avoids equating interim relief, bail or a printed statutory consolidation with repeal, acquittal or final constitutional validity.
gaps: Final appellate treatment, if any, of the IHC's 8 April 2022 Section 20 ruling.
Signed subsequent merits orders in the consolidated challenges to Act II of 2025 after the reported February hearing.
Certified July 2026 Toor order and subsequent inquiry outcome.
Signed Ghauri bail order, compliance with surety conditions and subsequent prosecution outcome.
Separate disposal records for the original Toor, Absar Alam, Ghauri and Fawad Ali Shah matters; new FIRs do not resolve old ones.

reports.title: Tunisia v. Emna Chargui: Follow-Up to the June 2021 TrialWatch Report
reports.status_label: Conviction appealed; subsequent appellate disposition unverified
reports.status_qualification: The dated conviction is taken from the original report. The original also confirms an appeal and asylum in Germany by June 2021, without precise event dates. No later case-disposing order was verified through 9 October 2026. Amnesty's 15 July 2020 article describes sentencing 'yesterday', conflicting with the original's 13 July date.
executive: The latest precisely dated judicial event established in the examined record is Chargui's July 2020 first-instance conviction: the original gives 13 July, six months' imprisonment and a TND 2,000 fine. By June 2021, it recorded an appeal and asylum in Germany. Subsequent research did not establish an appellate judgment, pardon, retrial or enforcement outcome. CFJ's later online publication is a report listing, not evidence of a new court decision. [O] [S3]

Accordingly, this update cannot describe the conviction as overturned, finally upheld or served. Nor does a six-month sentence establish present liberty. The original D grade was assigned by TrialWatch expert Knox Thames; no new grade is assigned here. [O]
baseline: The prosecution concerned a Facebook post in May 2020 reproducing a satirical public-health text in the form of a Quranic verse. Chargui was prosecuted under Articles 52 and 53 of Decree 115 of 2011, concerning incitement of religious hatred and interference with authorized religious observance. The report distinguished an irreverent expression from evidence of incitement to violence or a demonstrable threat to others. [O]

TrialWatch identified restrictions on access to counsel during questioning, shortcomings in the prosecution's presentation of evidence, and concerns about legality, freedom of expression and the presumption of innocence. It reported that counsel appealed within the statutory period, but that her absence from Tunisia complicated participation in the appeal. Those are historical findings and procedural descriptions from June 2021, not independently established descriptions of a proceeding still pending in 2026. [O]

timeline.event: Satirical public-health text shared on Facebook; exact posting day differs between accounts.
First-instance conviction dated 13 July in the original; Amnesty's contemporary account implies 14 July.
Original report records an appeal and asylum in Germany; their precise dates are not supplied.
CFJ announces its Tunisia reports; this is a publication, not appellate adjudication.
CFJ report-page publication metadata; underlying PDF remains dated June 2021.

developments: Amnesty's contemporary statement reported that Chargui was at liberty and intended to appeal in July 2020. It urged reversal of the conviction and investigation of threats against her. reports.title: Bangladesh v. Shahidul Alam: Investigation Stayed in 2024 and Case Quashed in 2025
reports.status_label: High Court quashed case on 7 August 2025; subsequent appellate position unverified
reports.status_qualification: Quashing is corroborated by local court reporting and Amnesty. No later State appeal, leave application, stay or appellate disposition was verified. The 2022 appellate proceedings concerned an earlier challenge and must not be mistaken for an appeal from the 2025 order.
executive: The latest verified case-disposing event is the High Court's 7 August 2025 quashing of the ICT Act case against Shahidul Alam, corroborated by contemporaneous local reporting and Amnesty the following day. This followed a November 2024 stay of the investigation. A subsequent appeal or stay against the quashing was not established through 9 October 2026, so unconditional finality should not be claimed. [S1] [S2] [S3]

The relief is distinct from Alam's release on bail in 2018 and from an acquittal after trial. It changes the prosecution's legal posture, while not itself establishing compensation or accountability for alleged mistreatment. The January 2023 original assigned no letter grade. [O]
baseline: Alam was arrested on 5 August 2018 after public commentary and an Al Jazeera interview concerning student road-safety protests. A case under ICT Act Section 57 followed. The original examined the speech allegations, detention, alleged torture and the consequences of Section 57's repeal and statutory savings provisions. It argued that the prosecution should not continue where the relevant savings provision did not preserve an investigation at that stage. That argument was not itself a court disposal. [O]

The report also traced an earlier challenge: a 2021 High Court ruling on maintainability and rejection of leave by the Appellate Division on 27 November 2022. Accordingly, when the original appeared in January 2023, it could not report the later 2024 stay or 2025 quashing. References to the 2022 appeal in subsequent coverage describe this earlier litigation, not a proven State appeal from the 2025 order. [O]

developments: Dhaka Tribune reported that the High Court suspended the investigation on 4 November 2024 and issued a rule calling for justification of its continuation. A rule to show cause is not yet a final quashing order. The report therefore supplies a genuine intermediate development without establishing that the prosecution had already ended in 2024. [S1]

New Age reported that the High Court quashed the case on 7 August 2025. Bangla-language Ajker Patrika independently reported the order, identified the bench of Justices Mustafa Zaman Islam and Tamanna Rahman Khalidi, and described the rule as made absolute. These accounts support an actual judicial disposal, not simply counsel's hope that the proceedings would be withdrawn. The signed reasons were not obtained, so the precise ratio and operative scope should not be reconstructed from the original report's legal argument. [S2] [S4]

Amnesty welcomed the dismissal on 8 August and reiterated its assessment that the prosecution arose from protected expression. It also called for remedies for the arrest and alleged torture. Those are attributed NGO assessments and demands, not a demonstrated judicial award. Amnesty's chronology distinguishes the 15 November 2018 bail order from release on 20 November, an important separation when describing liberty. [S3]
analysis: Analytical inference: the new order materially supersedes the original's description of an investigation permitted to continue following the earlier unsuccessful challenge. The change is not merely a better national political climate; it is a reported case-specific judicial act. The November stay and August quashing must therefore be treated as separate procedural stages. [O] [S1] [S2]

Analytical inference: quashing removes the case on the reported High Court order, but a verified finality claim requires checking any subsequent State leave application and stay. Searching for a later appeal did not establish one; results about the 2022 appeal cannot answer that question. Absence of a located appeal is not proof that no appeal exists. [O]

Analytical inference: termination of the prosecution and redress for detention or mistreatment are distinct issues. A favorable disposal does not establish compensation, a finding of torture or proceedings against those responsible. Those questions remain open absent separate remedial records. [S3]
conclusion: The follow-up should report the verified 7 August 2025 quashing prominently, while qualifying any statement about subsequent appellate finality. It should preserve the distinction between the earlier release on bail, termination of the case and unresolved accountability claims. [S2] [S3]
gaps: Signed 7 August 2025 High Court judgment, case number, reasons and exact operative scope.
Whether the State filed a leave-to-appeal application against that order, and whether any stay or subsequent decision was issued.
Any compensation, torture investigation or other remedial proceedings and their outcomes.
Current registry confirmation rather than reliance on older appeals or retrospective NGO summaries.

reports.title: Belarus v. Katsiaryna Andreyeva and Daria Chultsova
reports.original_grade: D (Beth Van Schaack, original TrialWatch assessment)
reports.category: Release after sentence / pardon; separate subsequent prosecution
reports.status_label: Chultsova released in 2022; Andreyeva pardoned and released in March 2026
reports.status_qualification: Latest dated follow-up is PEN International's 24 March response to the 19 March release. Chultsova's September 2022 release followed completion of her term; Andreyeva's 2026 release followed a pardon after a separate treason conviction. Neither event establishes that either original conviction was quashed.
executive: Katsiaryna Andreyeva was pardoned and released on 19 March 2026, after more than five years in custody. CPJ confirmed her transfer to Lithuania; PEN International's 24 March statement subsequently addressed the release and exile of the freed group. This was not a 2025 pardon or an acquittal. [S4] [S5]

Daria Chultsova had already been released in September 2022 after serving her sentence. A September 2025 Belarusian Association of Journalists report placed her in Poland. The defendants therefore have different post-report trajectories, despite sharing the prosecution monitored in 2021. [S3] [S6]
baseline: The October 2021 report examined the prosecution arising from the journalists' live coverage of a memorial protest for Raman Bandarenka on 15 November 2020. Andreyeva was reporting and Chultsova operating the camera from an apartment overlooking the gathering. The Frunzensky District Court in Minsk convicted both under Article 342, concerning actions grossly violating public order, and imposed two-year prison sentences on 18 February 2021. [O]

TrialWatch expert Beth Van Schaack assigned the monitored proceedings a D. The report questioned the equation of journalism with protest organization, the evidentiary basis for attributing transport disruption to the defendants, restrictions on defense questioning and documentary evidence, and judicial impartiality and the presumption of innocence. That assessment concerned the February 2021 hearings. It did not monitor the later closed treason proceedings against Andreyeva. [O]

timeline.event: Both defendants convicted and sentenced to two years in the monitored public-order case.
Andreyeva convicted of treason in a separate closed proceeding; CPJ reported an additional eight-year sentence.
Chultsova released after serving her term; BAJ published confirmation on 5 September.
BAJ reported the Supreme Court upheld Andreyeva's effective sentence of eight years and three months.
BAJ's dated reporting described Chultsova as living in Poland.
Andreyeva pardoned, released and transferred to Lithuania.
PEN International condemned the forced exile accompanying the recent releases.

developments: Andreyeva's continued imprisonment was not simply the original two-year term running its course. CPJ reported that a court in Homel convicted her of treason on 13 July 2022 after a closed trial. Details of the alleged conduct were not publicly established in that account. The additional prosecution must be treated independently of the public-order charges and the evidence examined by TrialWatch. [S1]

On 20 September 2022, BAJ reported an unsuccessful Supreme Court appeal and an effective sentence of eight years and three months. Citing Andreyeva's husband, it said the description of the treason allegation changed from disclosure of state secrets to espionage without changing the outcome. This is an attributed account, not independent access to the sealed judgment. [S2]

BAJ confirmed Chultsova's release in early September 2022 after completion of her sentence. Public sources vary over the precise day; this report uses the month rather than converting BAJ's publication date into a release date. Her later presence in Poland is separately documented, rather than inferred from the original sentence length. [S3] [S6]

CPJ linked the March release to a negotiated package and confirmed Andreyeva's pardon and transfer to Lithuania without passports. PEN International welcomed release but characterized the accompanying exile as coercive. These assessments are attributed to those organizations. [S4] [S5]
analysis: Analytical inference: the shared trial no longer supplies a single status for both defendants. Completion of Chultsova's term and Andreyeva's later pardon are legally different routes out of custody. The separate treason case explains why the original two-year sentence cannot establish Andreyeva's release date. [O] [S1] [S3] [S4]

Analytical inference: release improves physical liberty without establishing judicial rehabilitation. A pardon does not validate the trial or establish innocence. Reported forced departure also prevents an assumption of unconditional restoration of the journalists' previous lives. [S4] [S5]
conclusion: Both defendants have verified releases, reached through different procedures. The follow-up should preserve the original attributed grade, describe the later treason case separately, and leave the continuing legal effects of both convictions expressly unresolved.
gaps: Exact day of Chultsova's September 2022 release: contemporaneous accounts and later profiles differ between 3 and 5 September.
Full judgments and publicly reviewable evidence in Andreyeva's treason proceedings, including the precise calculation of the reported eight-year-three-month effective sentence.
Scope and legal conditions of Andreyeva's individual pardon, including whether criminal records, civil restrictions or return rights changed.
Any subsequent judgment vacating either defendant's 2021 conviction; no such disposition was verified through the cutoff.

reports.title: Georgia v. Mzia Amaglobeli
reports.original_grade: D (Sir Nicolas Bratza, original TrialWatch assessment)
reports.status_label: Reported imprisoned; Supreme Court declined cassation; ECHR complaints filed
reports.status_qualification: 21 September is the publication date of a CMIS report covering September 2025-August 2026, not a new detention order. Latest verified domestic criminal disposition: Supreme Court nonadmission on 4 March 2026. A conviction-related ECHR application was reportedly filed 26 June and registered 3 July. No release or ECHR merits judgment was verified through 9 October.
executive: The Supreme Court declined to admit Amaglobeli's cassation appeal on 4 March 2026; this was not a new merits judgment. Subsequent reporting confirms that the previously planned Strasbourg challenge to the conviction became an actual application, filed on 26 June and registered on 3 July. [S1] [S4]

The latest specific account located, published by CMIS on 21 September 2026 and covering developments through August, described her as imprisoned, reported refusal of early release, and counted four European Court of Human Rights applications. Registration of those complaints does not itself establish admissibility, a violation or release. [S6]
baseline: The January 2026 original concerned Amaglobeli, founder of Batumelebi and Netgazeti, following her arrest during protests in Batumi in January 2025. The prosecution initially charged an attack on a police officer. On 6 August 2025 the court convicted her instead under Article 353(1), concerning resistance to an officer, and sentenced her to two years. The Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld that result on 18 November 2025. The original already covered those appellate hearings; they are not post-report discoveries. [O]

TrialWatch expert Sir Nicolas Bratza assigned a D. The assessment identified inadequate notice of the substituted charge, impaired access to defense materials and witnesses, participation problems associated with the courtroom glass enclosure, prejudicial statements by public officials, and inadequate justification for imprisonment. This follow-up attributes those findings to the original report rather than issuing a new grade or independently adopting every allegation as judicially established. [O]

timeline.event: Conviction on the substituted Article 353(1) charge and two-year sentence.
Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld conviction and sentence.
GYLA reported two already-filed Strasbourg cases, concerning detention rather than the later cassation disposition.
Supreme Court declined admission of cassation; a separate ill-treatment ECHR application was also filed that day.

Conviction and fair-trial application submitted, according to GYLA as reported by The Messenger.
Fourth application registered, according to the same report.
Georgia Today published Amaglobeli's prison letter awaiting international justice.
CMIS published its through-August review reporting imprisonment, early-release refusal and four Strasbourg applications.

developments: CPJ reported nonadmission on 4 March, citing her lawyers' criticism that the Supreme Court had not addressed their admissibility arguments. CPJ also recorded an intention to appeal to Strasbourg. That statement alone would not prove a filing; the later records must supply the missing procedural step. [S1]

GYLA's 14 January update identified two different Strasbourg proceedings already in existence: application 13661/25, filed on 28 April 2025 concerning criminal detention, and application 36304/25, filed on 17 November 2025 concerning administrative detention. In the first, the government had submitted observations in October 2025 and GYLA had responded by January. The alleged violations were the applicants' claims, not Strasbourg findings. [S2]

Batumelebi reported a third application alleging police ill-treatment and deficiencies in its investigation. It was submitted on 4 March 2026 and registered on 11 March, with notification received on 1 April. Sharing a date with the Supreme Court decision does not make this complaint the conviction appeal. [S3]

The Messenger subsequently reported GYLA's announcement of a fourth complaint: the conviction and fair-trial challenge, submitted on 26 June and registered on 3 July. It concerned the prosecution and proceedings at all three domestic court levels. The account identified GYLA and Edward Fitzgerald as representatives. The filing is verified through reporting of counsel's statement, not an independently retrieved Strasbourg docket. [S4]

In a prison letter published on 11 September, Amaglobeli said she was awaiting international justice and rejected seeking a pardon through an apology. CMIS's later publication also reported refusal of early release and obstacles to visiting her. Neither source identifies a subsequent favorable judgment; the precise early-release decision date and written reasons remain unverified. [S5] [S6]
analysis: Analytical inference: the strongest procedural change is a move from domestic cassation nonadmission to an actually filed international challenge. The four applications must not be collapsed into one: detention, administrative detention, ill-treatment and the conviction raise different factual and procedural questions. Their existence is evidence of litigation, not success in that litigation. [S2] [S3] [S4]

Analytical inference: a two-year sentence cannot be used to calculate present liberty or a guaranteed release day. The available later accounts still described imprisonment. Any future report should obtain a specific custody or release record and identify the outcome of each Strasbourg case separately before changing that characterization. [S5] [S6]
conclusion: The verified follow-up is unsuccessful access to domestic cassation and multiple actual Strasbourg applications, including the conviction challenge. The public record located does not justify describing Amaglobeli as released, pardoned or exonerated.
gaps: Supreme Court's complete nonadmission order and precise admissibility reasoning.
Application number and official procedural status of the June 2026 conviction complaint and March 2026 ill-treatment complaint.
Any ECHR admissibility, interim-measure or merits ruling; registration is not such a ruling.
Date, decision-maker, written reasons and review status of the reported early-release refusal.
Custody confirmation covering the interval after the September publication through 9 October, or any intervening release order.

reports.title: Guatemala v. Jose Ruben Zamora
reports.category: House arrest; repeated custody reversals; retrial pending
reports.status_label: Under house arrest; renewed annulment and retrial order; foreign travel refused
reports.status_qualification: National Press Club's 8 October 2026 statement explicitly confirms ongoing house arrest. Latest substantive judicial development located is the 13 August refusal to lift his exit restriction. July finality applies to the particular withdrawn appeal over substitute measures, not to the criminal prosecution or retrial.
executive: Zamora remained under house arrest on 8 October 2026, according to the National Press Club's award announcement. This is the latest specific custody confirmation found before the research cutoff, and is not unconditional release or an acquittal. [S6]

July brought two separate outcomes: withdrawal of the constitutional challenge to substitute custody measures, and renewed annulment with a retrial order. On 13 August the court refused medical travel abroad; reporting then said the retrial had not begun. [S3] [S4] [S5]
baseline: The February 2024 report concerned the founder of elPeriodico, arrested on 29 July 2022 and tried for money laundering, influence peddling and blackmail. In June 2023 he received a six-year money-laundering sentence and was acquitted of the other two charges. In October 2023 an appeals court annulled both the conviction and acquittals and ordered a retrial. At publication, cassation proceedings remained pending; the report did not establish a final conviction. [O]

TrialWatch expert Camilo Sanchez assigned an F. The report identified serious restrictions on defense evidence, treatment of the burden of proof, interference with legal representation and deficiencies in the review and conditions of detention. Several defense lawyers themselves faced proceedings. The shutdown of elPeriodico in May 2023 formed part of the documented consequences. The later history must therefore track custody, evidentiary remedies and the merits separately rather than treating every release decision as resolution of the criminal case. [O]

timeline.event: Six-year laundering conviction and acquittals on two other charges.
Original judgment annulled and retrial ordered; already covered by the baseline.
Zamora actually moved to house arrest; prosecutors challenged the measure.

Zamora returned to prison following that reversal.
CPJ confirmed renewed release from prison to house arrest.
Supreme Court granted amparo restoring substitute measures, as subsequently reported.
Reporting confirmed acceptance of prosecutors' withdrawn constitutional appeal and a separate renewed annulment/retrial order; exact underlying order dates require full decisions.
Tribunal Noveno refused removal of exit restriction for medical travel.
National Press Club explicitly confirmed continuing house arrest in award announcement.

developments: The route out of prison was reversible. AP's March 2025 account recorded actual house arrest in October 2024, an adverse appellate ruling in November, and return to prison on 10 March 2025. On 12 February 2026 CPJ confirmed another move to house arrest while the criminal proceedings continued. None of these custody decisions alone disposed of the allegations. [S2] [S1]

On 28 July, Prensa Libre reported acceptance of the prosecution's total withdrawal of its constitutional appeal. The challenged Supreme Court amparo, granted on 20 March, had restored substitute measures. The withdrawn appeal could not be renewed. This particular proceeding ended, not the prosecution or all possible custody litigation. [S3]

In a separate report the same day, Prensa Comunitaria described a renewed appellate annulment of the 2023 judgment and referral for retrial before Tribunal Noveno. It followed a reported October 2025 Criminal Chamber instruction to reconsider the appellate reasoning. The article also discussed the treatment of excluded defense evidence and co-defendant Samari Gomez. The full operative decision is needed to establish the exact scope of the retrial and any unresolved challenges. [S4]

On 13 August, Prensa Libre reported a majority refusal to lift Zamora's exit restriction for medical treatment in Florida, although prosecutors did not oppose the request. The court considered the proposed treatment insufficiently urgent. The same report said the retrial had not started and that Gomez had challenged the retrial order on 11 August; separating their proceedings was refused. These are attributed accounts of ongoing litigation, not proof that a new trial had concluded. [S5]

The National Press Club's 8 October statement supplies a more recent custody check than the February release announcement. It named Zamora as a press-freedom award recipient while explicitly describing continuing house arrest and the defense of outstanding charges. The proposed November award ceremony was still future at the cutoff and is not treated as an event already held. [S6]
analysis: Analytical inference: the central follow-up is an unresolved merits case accompanied by repeated changes in coercive measures. July's procedural finality concerning one withdrawn appeal should not be generalized into a final acquittal, irrevocable freedom or an end to the retrial. [S3] [S4]

Analytical inference: removing a judgment does not necessarily cure the original report's defects. A future retrial must be assessed for evidence access, representation and delay. House arrest and an exit ban remain liberty restrictions despite being less severe than imprisonment. [O] [S5]
conclusion: As of the cutoff, the best-supported characterization is house arrest with ongoing criminal proceedings and a reported retrial order. There is no verified retrial verdict or unconditional release. The most recent confirmation is dated 8 October, not the earlier February custody decision.
gaps: Certified July appellate and constitutional decisions, including their exact issuance dates and operative scope.
Disposition of Gomez's reported 11 August challenge and its effect on Zamora's retrial timetable.
Whether the retrial began after 13 August, which charges remain for retrial, and which defense evidence is admissible.
Current conditions of house arrest, exit restriction and any other independent pending prosecutions.
Any later medical-travel authorization, unconditional release, dismissal or retrial judgment before the cutoff; none was verified.

reports.title: Hong Kong Special Administrative Region v. Bao Choy Yuk-ling
reports.category: Convictions quashed; later distinct registry-policy litigation
reports.status_label: Both convictions quashed by Court of Final Appeal in June 2023
reports.status_qualification: Latest related judicial event is a separate March 2026 judicial review of the revised vehicle-records policy. It did not reinstate Choy's convictions. Her criminal appeal was allowed on 5 June 2023 in FACC 2/2023, [2023] HKCFA 12.
executive: On 5 June 2023, the Court of Final Appeal unanimously quashed both convictions and set aside Choy's sentence: a judicial reversal, not a pardon. [S2]

The latest related judgment located, dated 6 March 2026, dismissed the Hong Kong Journalists Association's challenge to a revised vehicle-records access policy. That separate administrative case does not reverse Choy's successful criminal appeal. [S4] [S5]
baseline: The July 2021 report concerned Choy's use of vehicle-registration records for an RTHK documentary investigating the 21 July 2019 Yuen Long attacks and the police response. The application form required a declared purpose; she selected the catch-all category for other traffic-and-transport-related matters. Authorities subsequently treated that declaration as false. She was arrested in November 2020, convicted on two false-statement charges in 2021 and fined HK$6,000. Her appeal was pending at the report's publication. [O]

The original expert assigned a C. TrialWatch considered courtroom procedures generally fair, while identifying concerns about the legal clarity of the form and offence and the apparent selective targeting of public-interest journalism. Those concerns were an assessment of the monitored trial, not a prediction of the later appellate result. The follow-up therefore distinguishes the original grading exercise from the binding interpretation subsequently supplied by the Court of Final Appeal. [O]

timeline.event: Original report published while Choy's appeal remained pending.
Court of First Instance dismissed her initial criminal appeal.
Court of Final Appeal allowed appeal, quashed both convictions and set sentence aside.
Revised vehicle-records application arrangements implemented, as recorded in the later official judgment summary.
Transport Department explained specified purposes and exceptional public-interest application route.
Court of First Instance dismissed HKJA's separate challenge to the revised policy.

developments: The Court of First Instance initially dismissed the criminal appeal on 7 November 2022 in HCMA 236/2021, [2022] HKCFI 3343. It accepted a narrower relationship between the permitted search purpose and road-traffic use. This intermediate result matters because the eventual appellate success was not the first response to the conviction. [S1]

In FACC 2/2023, [2023] HKCFA 12, the court held that the catch-all purpose encompassed bona fide journalism. Even on the narrower interpretation, the ambiguous form did not establish guilty knowledge as the only reasonable inference. Materiality to the Commissioner's function did not itself prove falsity or knowledge. The operative order quashed both convictions and set aside the sentence. [S2]

The Transport Department's January 2024 statement described a redesigned application regime with specified purposes and written applications for exceptional public-interest uses. It presented the arrangements as balancing privacy and access, and as consistent with the earlier judgment. That is the government's stated rationale, not a determination that every later journalistic request must be approved. [S3]

The later judicial review, HCAL 559/2024, [2026] HKCFI 917, concerned HKJA and the Commissioner for Transport, not new false-statement charges against Choy. On 6 March 2026 the court dismissed the challenge. It identified errors in guidance and declarations requiring correction but did not grant the review. The official Department of Justice summary separately records the policy's January 2024 implementation and the review's disposition. [S4] [S5]
analysis: Analytical inference: the criminal judgment addressed proof of the particular offence on the old form, whereas the later litigation examined the lawfulness of a different access policy. Conflating the two would falsely suggest either that the 2023 result created unrestricted registry access or that the 2026 judgment restored Choy's convictions. [S2] [S4]

Analytical inference: the appellate reasoning addresses the original clarity concern without endorsing every TrialWatch assessment, particularly prosecutorial motive. The court's reasons and order, not the historical grade, determine the criminal disposition. [O] [S2]
conclusion: The original prosecution ended in the verified quashing of both convictions. Continuing disputes over journalists' registry access are important follow-up context, but remain a separate legal controversy with a separate judgment and unresolved questions about implementation.
gaps: Whether HKJA appealed the March 2026 judicial-review judgment and any later disposition before 9 October.
Implementation and timing of the corrections to guidance and declarations identified by the 2026 court.
Any verified fine refund, compensation or other personal remedial order beyond the CFA's quashing order.
Practical outcomes of Choy's or other journalists' applications under the revised policy; no unrestricted-access conclusion is supported.

reports.title: Kazakhstan v. Aigul Utepova
reports.status_label: UN individual communication registered; last confirmed pending in 2025; present restrictions unverified
reports.status_qualification: Latest verified procedural status appears in TrialWatch's submission for the June-July 2025 Human Rights Committee session: Aigul Utepova v. Kazakhstan, No. 4903/2023, pending. Exact submission day is unstated. This does not establish a UN merits decision, domestic reversal, release, termination of activity restrictions, or removal of banking restrictions as of October 2026.
executive: CFJ announced an actual UN complaint in April 2022. Its submission for the June-July 2025 Human Rights Committee session identifies Utepova's registered communication, No. 4903/2023, as pending: the latest verified procedural status. [S1] [S2]
Her present liberty and financial restrictions remain unverified; sentence duration cannot establish their termination.
baseline: The supplied April 2022 report concerns journalist Aigul Utepova's prosecution under Article 405(2) for alleged participation in the activities of banned opposition groups, the Democratic Choice of Kazakhstan and Koshe Party. The prosecution relied on political commentary and social-media activity; the report found no allegation that she advocated violence. She disputed that reporting or commenting on the groups amounted to participation in them. [O]

Following arrest in September 2020, she spent months under house arrest and underwent involuntary psychiatric confinement from 23 November to 11 December 2020. Release from the clinic was a distinct event and did not establish release from house arrest. The report examined the justification and safeguards for confinement as well as the later trial. [O]

On 29 April 2021, the trial court imposed one year of restricted movement, a two-year ban on social-media use and public activism, and 100 hours of compulsory labor. Her conviction appeal was rejected in June 2021. The report also documented inclusion on a terrorism-financing-related list and blocked bank access. These are historical findings, not verification that the same restraints remain active in 2026. [O]

TrialWatch expert Dr. Eva Szeli assigned the original grade D. The report identified pretrial and trial rights violations, problems with expert evidence and disclosure, and the vague, overbroad application of anti-extremism rules to nonviolent expression. The present follow-up attributes those conclusions to the original report without giving the case a new grade. [O]

timeline.event: Involuntary psychiatric confinement began; ended on 11 December, separately from house arrest.
Convicted and sentenced to restricted liberty, activity ban and compulsory labor.
Conviction appeal rejected, according to CPJ's account based on the ruling and journalist.
CFJ and Debevoise announced that a Human Rights Committee communication had been submitted.
2025 HRC submission: communication 4903/2023 pending.

developments: CFJ's April 2022 statement says the communication sought reversal of the conviction, an apology and reparations, as well as reform of anti-extremism laws. Those are the representatives' requested remedies, not relief already granted by the Committee. The same statement describes frozen bank access and health and professional harm as they were understood at that time. [S1]
The 2025 NGO submission confirms registration and then-pending status, not a Committee decision. Its session date, rather than later search indexing, dates the account. [S2]

CPJ's historical profile records rejection of the appeal on 1 June 2021 and says Utepova had not yet submitted her planned UN complaint as of October 2021. That earlier statement is consistent with a subsequent filing announced in April 2022, rather than evidence against it. The profile should not be read as a live prisoner-status record. [S4]
analysis: Analytical inference: registration is meaningful procedural progress, not success on admissibility, merits or implementation. [S2]

Analytical inference: post-sentence restrictions require independent verification. Restricted movement, a professional or speech ban, a criminal record, and financial-list measures need not end together. Accordingly, neither the passage of one or two years nor a historical NGO profile justifies declaring her free of restrictions or still confined. [O] [S3]
conclusion: The registered UN complaint was last confirmed pending in 2025. Later outcome and current personal circumstances remain unresolved. [S2]
gaps: Has the Human Rights Committee decided admissibility or merits in communication No. 4903/2023?
Was any domestic conviction review, pardon, expungement or other remedy granted?
What document confirms completion or termination of restricted liberty and the activity ban?
Is Utepova currently included on the financial-monitoring list, and has access to her bank accounts been restored?
Can counsel or the journalist provide a dated account of her present circumstances?

reports.title: Malaysia v. Malaysiakini and Steven Gan: Review Dismissed in March 2022
reports.status_label: Company's contempt conviction left in place after review dismissal; Gan acquitted
reports.status_qualification: The latest verified case-disposing event is rejection of the company's review application, not a new conviction of Gan. Payment of the original fine was reported. No subsequent reversal was verified; this does not independently establish exhaustion of every conceivable remedy.
executive: On 29 March 2022, a seven-member Federal Court panel unanimously dismissed Mkini Dotcom's application to review its contempt conviction and RM 500,000 fine. Reporting also confirms payment of the fine. The original acquittal of editor-in-chief Steven Gan must remain distinct from the company's unsuccessful review. No later reversal was verified through the research cutoff. [S1] [O]

This resolves the specific review anticipated in the October 2021 original, but should not be described as a fresh appellate trial or a personal prison sentence for Gan. TrialWatch expert Joan Barata assigned the original D grade; this update does not issue a replacement grade. [O] [S2]
baseline: The case concerned five reader comments posted under a June 2020 Malaysiakini article about the reopening of courts. On 19 February 2021, the Federal Court found the publishing company guilty of contempt by a six-to-one majority and imposed a RM 500,000 fine; it acquitted Gan. The original followed the July 2020 merits hearing and examined the subsequent judgment. [O]

The report criticized reliance on the Evidence Act Section 114A publication presumption and the treatment of a platform's responsibility for third-party comments. It analyzed whether the procedure and penalty complied with presumption-of-innocence and free-expression standards, including necessity and proportionality. Its international-law analysis did not make Malaysia an ICCPR state party. These are attributed TrialWatch criticisms, not findings adopted in the later review ruling. [O]

The original stated that a review hearing was expected on 12 October 2021. That was an anticipated procedural date, rather than a disposition. A follow-up must therefore identify the eventual review result and not merely repeat the scheduled hearing as though it resolved the matter. [O]

timeline.event: Article and third-party comments giving rise to contempt proceedings.
Company convicted and fined; Gan acquitted.
Review date anticipated in the original, not an established decision date.
Malaysiakini reports review rescheduled for 29 March.
Federal Court unanimously dismisses company's review; fine payment reported.

developments: Malaysiakini's January report recorded counsel's confirmation of a new March hearing date. The eventual March decision, rather than that announcement, provides the substantive procedural development after the original report. This sequence explains why the October 2021 scheduled date cannot serve as the endpoint of the follow-up. [S3]

Contemporaneous Bernama reporting states that the review panel found no breach of natural justice warranting reopening and regarded the arguments as already considered. It also reports no costs order because the matter involved public interest. Those conclusions explain rejection of this review request; they should not be expanded into an independent finding that every criticism in the TrialWatch report was answered. [S1]

The Vibes explains the restricted character of Federal Court review: it is not an ordinary appeal and does not authorize another hearing simply because a party disagrees with the result. It reports that the company complained about a lack of opportunity to address pivotal issues. The court nevertheless rejected reopening. This is an unsuccessful procedural challenge, distinct from the original substantive contempt adjudication. [S2]
analysis: Analytical inference: the review dismissal leaves the practical sanction and the original majority's approach to publisher responsibility in place in this case. It does not convert attributed fair-trial concerns into established violations, nor erase them solely because the threshold for exceptional review was not met. The original judgment and the review ruling answer related but different legal questions. [O] [S1] [S2]

Analytical inference: preserving the identity of the sanctioned legal person is essential. Treating the case title as proof that both respondents were convicted would incorrectly attach the company's liability to Gan. Likewise, a paid corporate fine supplies no basis for a claim that he was jailed, pardoned or released. [O]
conclusion: The specific review sought after the original report was dismissed on 29 March 2022. The verified position is an unreversed company conviction in the examined record and the separate original acquittal of Gan, without an assertion of unlimited legal finality. [S1] [O]
gaps: Full signed reasons for the 29 March 2022 review decision, beyond contemporaneous courtroom reporting.
Any later case-specific reopening, extraordinary remedy or order affecting the company conviction.
Any actual international filing and its outcome; neither a contemplated submission nor NGO criticism establishes one.

reports.title: Monitoring of the Trial of Marina Zolotova
reports.original_grade: C (ABA Center for Human Rights staff, original TrialWatch assessment)
reports.category: Separate later prosecution; pardon and release into exile
reports.status_label: Pardoned and released in December 2025; living in exile in 2026
reports.status_qualification: Latest related event is the release of later TUT.BY co-defendant Liudmila Chekina on 16 September 2026, not a new disposition for Zolotova. Zolotova's latest substantive personal account located is dated 7 August 2026. Her pardon and release do not establish that either conviction was overturned.
executive: Marina Zolotova, also transliterated Maryna Zolatava, was pardoned and released on 13 December 2025 after more than four years in custody in the later TUT.BY prosecution. In an account published by RSF Switzerland on 7 August 2026, she described life in exile in Poland and reunion with her family. [S2] [S3]

The latest related development verified before the cutoff is CPJ's 16 September 2026 confirmation that TUT.BY director and co-defendant Liudmila Chekina was also released. This does not alter the distinction between Zolotova's 2019 fine-only prosecution and the separate 2023 prison sentence. [S4] [O] [S1]
baseline: The July 2019 report concerned access by TUT.BY staff to material from the state-owned BeLTA news agency using shared subscription credentials. BeLTA temporarily restricted access to some stories before making them generally available. Zolotova, TUT.BY's editor-in-chief, was prosecuted for inaction by an official, based on an alleged failure to prevent the practice. Other people initially investigated were not tried alongside her. After a two-week trial in February 2019, she was convicted and fined rather than sentenced to imprisonment. [O]

ABA Center for Human Rights staff, acting as TrialWatch experts, assigned a C. The report considered the conduct of the trial largely fair but identified concerns about the purpose of singling out Zolotova and the reliability of pretrial statements. It could not assess a published reasoned judgment at the time. This historical report did not address the later raid on TUT.BY, the subsequent detention, or the closed national-security prosecution. [O]

timeline.event: Original TrialWatch report published on the fine-only BeLTA-related prosecution.
Zolotova arrested in the later investigation involving TUT.BY.
Minsk court imposed a twelve-year prison sentence in the separate later case.
Zolotova released among prisoners pardoned following negotiations with the United States.
RSF Switzerland published her account of exile, protection in Poland and family reunion.
CPJ confirmed release of later TUT.BY co-defendant Liudmila Chekina.

developments: Zolotova was arrested in May 2021, well after the monitored case. On 17 March 2023, CPJ reported a twelve-year sentence for inciting hatred and distributing calls aimed at harming national security following a closed trial. The initial tax-evasion allegation against her had been dropped. It is therefore inaccurate to describe her twelve-year sentence as either punishment for the 2019 BeLTA charge or a tax-evasion conviction. [S1]

CPJ's 15 December 2025 report confirmed that the release had occurred on 13 December, not merely that it was expected. It reported presidential pardons for the released group and placed Zolotova among them. CPJ welcomed her release while maintaining that her imprisonment was unjust. Its account supplies evidence of actual liberty from prison; it does not supply a judgment reversing the conviction. [S2]

In the RSF Switzerland account, Zolotova described being free since December but unable to return to her previous home. She explained the transfer through Ukraine into the European Union, obtaining international protection in Poland and reuniting with her family. This first-person account materially updates the immediate release announcement: it documents her circumstances months later rather than assuming that a pardon restored residence, work and family life in Belarus. [S3]

Chekina's situation must be dated separately. Although she remained imprisoned when the August account appeared, CPJ reported her release on 16 September among three freed journalists. The later event supersedes earlier descriptions of that co-defendant's custody. It should not be recast as a September release for Zolotova herself or as termination of the TUT.BY prosecution. [S4]
analysis: Analytical inference: one independent follow-up report can preserve the 2019 trial as its baseline while presenting the later prosecution as a distinct procedural history. Merging the two would obscure the different allegations, sanctions and evidentiary records, and would wrongly extend TrialWatch's monitoring to a closed trial it did not observe. [O] [S1]

Analytical inference: release and exile change the practical harm of imprisonment but do not answer the legality of the convictions. The absence of a verified quashing judgment is an evidentiary limit, not proof that every possible challenge failed. Chekina's later release updates a companion defendant's status without establishing Zolotova's legal rehabilitation. [S2] [S3] [S4]
conclusion: The verified outcome is freedom from imprisonment followed by documented life in exile, not an acquittal. The original C remains an attributed historical assessment of the 2019 proceedings; the later twelve-year sentence and presidential pardon require their own clearly separated account.
gaps: Published reasoned judgment and any appeal outcome in the 2019 BeLTA-related case.
Full judgment and verified completed appeal or review in the separate 2023 prosecution; a reported intention to appeal is insufficient.
Individual pardon instrument and its effects on convictions, civil disabilities, travel documents and return rights.
Any post-August 2026 substantive update on Zolotova's own legal status, distinct from Chekina's September release.

reports.title: Morocco v. Hajar Raissouni et al.: Pardon and the Unresolved Consequences of Conviction
reports.status_label: Pardoned in 2019; no subsequent acquittal or vacatur verified
reports.status_qualification: The latest located subject-specific follow-up is a published interview, not a new judicial disposition. The pardon and release occurred on 16 October 2019 and were already recorded in the original report. The record located through 9 October 2026 does not establish that the convictions were subsequently quashed.
executive: Hajar Raissouni and her co-defendants received a royal pardon on 16 October 2019. This was not a post-report development: the August 2020 TrialWatch report already distinguished the pardon from an acquittal. Amnesty International likewise reported that the convictions had not been quashed. The appropriate follow-up status is therefore pardon and release, without a verified later judicial clearing of the case. [O] [S1]

The latest located direct follow-up is Raissouni's interview published on 2 November 2022, describing post-release harassment and her subsequent life in Paris. Her earlier first-person account also described leaving Morocco. These accounts establish reported continuing consequences, not a new prosecution, a judicial finding of surveillance, or a 2026 determination of her circumstances. [S3] [S4]
baseline: The original report concerned five defendants arrested in connection with Raissouni's medical treatment on 31 August 2019: Raissouni, her fiance Rifaat Al Amine, doctor Jamal Belkeziz, anesthesiologist Mohamed Baba, and secretary Khadija Azelmadh. Raissouni was prosecuted for abortion and sexual relations outside marriage under Articles 454 and 490 of the Penal Code. On 30 September 2019, she and her fiance received one-year prison sentences; the doctor received two years; the other two defendants received suspended eight-month sentences. All five were pardoned on 16 October. [O]

TrialWatch expert Baroness Helena Kennedy assigned the proceedings a D grade. The report identified an invasive medical examination without consent, impediments to counsel, judicial impartiality concerns, contested police statements treated as confessions, and restrictions on defense evidence. Its assessment that the prosecution implicated discriminatory enforcement and Raissouni's journalism is the original expert's assessment, not a newly established judicial finding. The report explicitly stated that pardon did not erase conviction. [O]

timeline.event: Raissouni and the other defendants were arrested in connection with her medical treatment.
MENA Rights Group submitted the situation to seven UN Special Procedures mandates, according to its case profile.
The court convicted the five defendants. A UN Special Procedures communication was also issued on this date; these are separate actions.
Royal pardon of all five defendants; release of the imprisoned defendants. No acquittal was recorded.
Original TrialWatch report published, already incorporating the pardon.
MENA Rights Group updated its profile, identifying Raissouni as free and recording the earlier UN intervention.
Raissouni's first-person essay described post-release harassment and departure from Morocco.
A published interview with Raissouni described continuing pressure after release and her life in Paris.

developments: The 2021 MENA Rights Group update documents an actual September 2019 submission and a subsequent Special Procedures communication, rather than merely an intention to seek UN assistance. Both actions preceded the original report. The profile's later update confirms the release classification but does not supply a subsequent court judgment or a UN merits decision. [S2]

In her August 2021 essay, Raissouni described harassment after release, an initial obstacle to leaving Morocco that was later resolved, and continued attacks while abroad. She also discussed her and her husband's numbers appearing in leaked Pegasus-related records. That account should not be converted into a claim of independently verified infection of either device. [S3]

The November 2022 interview provides a later personal account of surveillance-like pressure following the pardon and relocation abroad. The source's introductory wording associates release with 17 October, whereas the original report and Amnesty identify 16 October as the operative pardon/release date. This follow-up retains the better-corroborated date and treats the interview as evidence of her reported experience, not adjudicated responsibility. [O] [S1] [S4]
analysis: Analytical inference: the decisive distinction is between ending imprisonment and correcting the legal record. Because the original report and Amnesty expressly distinguished pardon from quashing, an account describing the case simply as overturned would be misleading. A later rehabilitation, appeal judgment, or record-clearing measure would require its own evidence; none was located in the bounded searches. [O] [S1]
