reports.title: Uganda v. Moses Bwayo: Dismissal for Want of Prosecution and Later Exile
reports.category: Dismissal; subsequent safety and exile consequences
reports.status_label: Charge dismissed in August 2020; no reinstatement verified
reports.status_qualification: The latest verified follow-up is an official film-program announcement crediting Bwayo, not a court outcome. Dismissal for want of prosecution on 10 August 2020 was already in the original. His April 2024 first-person account places his move to the United States in March 2022 and describes seeking asylum; a grant was not verified. A same-name Ugandan civil case is an unconfirmed lead, not an attributed lawsuit or judgment.
executive: Moses Bwayo's unlawful-assembly prosecution was dismissed for want of prosecution on 10 August 2020. This was already the result recorded in the January 2021 TrialWatch report, not a later acquittal. No reinstatement or appeal of that dismissal was verified in the searches through 9 October 2026. [O]

The material post-report development is Bwayo's reported departure from Uganda. His April 2024 first-person account dates his move to the United States to March 2022 and describes seeking asylum. The latest verified follow-up, a Sundance announcement of 10 December 2025, credits him as a producer of a film selected for the 2026 festival. It establishes continued professional activity, not a new legal disposition or an asylum grant. [S3] [S4]
baseline: Bwayo was filming opposition politician and musician Robert Kyagulanyi, known as Bobi Wine, on a Kampala hotel rooftop on 24 February 2020 when police detained him. He was released on police bond on 26 February, arrested again and charged on 4 March with eight other people, remanded to Luzira Prison, and granted bail on 6 March. The charge was unlawful assembly. On 10 August, the Makindye Chief Magistrate's Court declined another adjournment and dismissed the prosecution after witnesses failed to appear. [O]

The ABA Center for Human Rights staff experts assigned the proceedings a C grade. The report identified concerns about the arrests, detention, charging basis and prosecution's failure to advance the case. Dismissal was not a merits judgment establishing innocence. The original also discussed Bwayo being shot in the face while filming in November 2020; because that event preceded the report, it must not be presented as newly discovered post-report violence. [O]

timeline.event: Detention while filming Bobi Wine; police bond followed on 26 February.
Rearrest, unlawful-assembly charge and remand; bail followed on 6 March.
Court dismissed the charge for want of prosecution.
Shooting while filming, already described in the original report.
Original TrialWatch report published, including dismissal and subsequent 2020 violence.
ABA webpage published the report summary; not a new dismissal date.
Move to the United States, retrospectively dated in Bwayo's April 2024 essay.
Irish Times profile reported departure from Uganda and seeking asylum, and recalled the dropped prosecution.
Bwayo published a first-person account of flight, threats and seeking asylum.
Sundance's 2026 selection announcement credited Bwayo as a KikuyuLand producer.

developments: ABA's July 2021 webpage reiterates the historical dismissal. It is a later publication of the existing result, not evidence of a second proceeding. The November 2023 Irish Times profile independently recalls that the case was eventually dropped, while reporting that Bwayo had left Uganda and was seeking asylum in the United States. It also describes interference with his filmmaking. [S1] [S2]

Bwayo's April 2024 essay supplies the more specific March 2022 relocation date. He describes threats, two attempted kidnappings of his wife, and the risks of return. These are attributed firsthand allegations, not adjudicated findings. His reference to seeking asylum supports an application-stage description only; the research did not establish a grant. The official Sundance selection announcement later supplies independent evidence of continued film work. [S3] [S4]

A Ugandan High Court cause list generated on 7 November 2025 names a Moses Bwayo against the Inspector General of Police and Attorney General in civil matter HCT-00-CV-MC-0019-2022, seeking declaratory orders and costs. This is an unresolved identity and linkage lead. No located pleading or judgment establishes that the claimant is this filmmaker or that the claim concerns the 2020 arrest. A cause list does not prove that the listed hearing occurred or disclose an outcome. It is therefore excluded from the verified case chronology. [S5]
analysis: Analytical inference: termination of this prosecution and safety after termination are separate questions. The original's dismissal establishes that the charge did not proceed at that point. Later flight accounts explain why that procedural outcome cannot be treated as restoration of safe working conditions. Neither flight nor the absence of a located reinstatement decision establishes the present status of every possible proceeding. [O] [S2] [S3]

Analytical inference: dismissal for want of prosecution should not be called an acquittal on the evidence. Nor should the same-name civil listing be upgraded into a successful rights claim, a damages award, or even a verified filing by this subject. The necessary missing link is an attributable case document identifying the claimant and the underlying incident. [O] [S5]
conclusion: The supported legal status remains the original August 2020 dismissal, with later reported exile and continued filmmaking. Retain the original C grade with attribution. Further conclusions about reinstatement, asylum status or civil redress require records not obtained in this research. [O] [S3] [S4]
gaps: Was the unlawful-assembly charge ever reinstated, or was the dismissal challenged? Obtain the later Makindye docket entries.
What is the current asylum status? Seeking asylum in the 2023-2024 accounts is not evidence that it was granted.
Is the claimant in HCT-00-CV-MC-0019-2022 the filmmaker, and does the matter concern the arrests monitored by TrialWatch? Obtain the originating motion and any ruling before attributing it.
Was there an investigation, accountability decision or compensation concerning the arrests or November 2020 shooting? No attributable outcome was verified.
Did any of the eight co-accused have a different subsequent outcome? The subject-focused later sources do not establish their status.

reports.title: Malaysia v. Dian Abdullah: Guilty Plea, Fine and Subsequent Section 233 Litigation
reports.original_path: /Users/xuxu/Downloads/Citizen Journalism/Malaysia_ A Preliminary Report on Criminal Proceedings Against Blogger Dian Abdullah.pdf
reports.status_label: Guilty plea and RM 10,000 fine reported in December 2021
reports.status_qualification: Personal-case event: sentencing on 21 December 2021, following a guilty plea on 6 December. Fine payment, default imprisonment and later appeal were not verified. Section 233 developments through 6 February 2026 concern separate constitutional litigation and do not establish reversal of Dian's conviction.
executive: Research under Dian Abdullah's legal-name variant, Lai Yuet Ming, establishes a post-report disposition: Bernama reported a change to guilty pleas on 6 December 2021 and total fines of RM 10,000 on 21 December. CIJ explicitly identifies Lai Yuet Ming as Dian Abdullah, connecting the reporting to the original case rather than merely a similar prosecution. Payment and any later appeal remain unverified. [S1] [S2]

The latest relevant legal-framework event is the Federal Court's 6 February 2026 decision in Government of Malaysia v. Heidy Quah Gaik Li, reversing the invalidation of the pre-amendment Section 233 terms 'offensive' and 'annoy'. That judgment concerned another litigant; it is not a judgment disposing of Dian's case. The original preliminary report assigned no letter grade. [S4] [O]
baseline: The original, dated 24 March 2021, examined proceedings over two Malaysia Flip Flop posts in March 2020 concerning the king's appointment of Muhyiddin Yassin and the prime minister's pandemic response. Charges brought in June 2020 relied on Penal Code Section 505(b) and Communications and Multimedia Act Section 233(1)(a). Bail was set at RM 4,000. [O]

Trial hearings began in December 2020. The preliminary report questioned whether testimony established public harm or incitement, rather than official discomfort with critical language. It recorded another hearing scheduled for 25 March 2021; that schedule did not determine the eventual outcome. The international free-expression standards discussed in the report should not be presented as proof that Malaysia is an ICCPR state party. [O]

timeline.event: First post later charged under Penal Code Section 505(b).
Second post later charged under Section 233(1)(a).
Charges brought; CIJ identifies Lai Yuet Ming as Dian Abdullah.
Changed pleas to guilty, according to subsequent Bernama sentencing coverage.
Sentenced to fines totaling RM 10,000, with imprisonment in default of payment.
Separate statutory development: amended Section 233 uses 'grossly offensive'.
Separate Quah litigation: Court of Appeal invalidates two pre-amendment terms, as dated in the later Federal Court judgment; appellate report heading instead bears 26 August.
Federal Court partly allows government's Quah appeal and restores the impugned terms.

developments: The sentencing report separates the fines: RM 4,000 for the Section 233 count and RM 6,000 for Section 505(b), with three and six months' imprisonment respectively in default. It does not establish that the fine was paid or default custody occurred. The verified change is therefore a reported plea-based conviction and financial sentence, not an acquittal or confirmed period of imprisonment. [S2]

The 2025 Court of Appeal judgment in Quah found the pre-amendment criminalization of offensive communications intended to annoy inconsistent with constitutional free-expression guarantees. Its decision was prospective. That limitation alone prevents treating the ruling as an automatic reopening of earlier convictions, and the constitutional position subsequently changed on appeal. [S3]

The Federal Court partly allowed the government's appeal in February 2026. It treated the abstract constitutional challenge as inappropriate after Quah's discharge and the prosecution's no-further-action decision, and upheld the impugned statutory language. Nevertheless, it found her particular post protected and lacking the relevant intent. The case therefore does not authorize an inference that every critical or disagreeable communication satisfies Section 233. [S4]
analysis: Analytical inference: a guilty plea changes the procedural question from whether the unfinished monitored trial proved guilt to whether the plea, conviction and sentence were lawfully entered and enforced. The public sentencing account does not supply a plea transcript or establish that the report's earlier fairness concerns were resolved. [O] [S2]

Analytical inference: the Quah litigation is relevant to the statutory theory criticized in the original, but not evidence of individual relief for Dian. The applicable version of the law, prospective effect, intent element and availability of any procedural remedy would each require separate analysis. Restoring wording in a different case neither validates the original trial procedure nor changes a recorded fine by itself. [S3] [S4]
conclusion: The personal case progressed beyond the preliminary report to a reported guilty plea and sentence. Any follow-up should record that disposition while leaving payment, enforcement and further challenge open. Later constitutional litigation belongs in a separately identified legal-framework section.
gaps: Signed plea and sentencing records for both counts, including reasons for the plea change.
Fine-payment receipt and any default-imprisonment order or custody record.
Any appeal, revision, pardon or application invoking subsequent Section 233 litigation.
Reconciliation of the Quah appellate judgment heading's 26 August date with the Federal Court's 19 August account.

reports.title: Tunisia v. Myriam Bribri: Conviction and the Unverified Appellate Outcome
reports.status_label: December 2021 conviction appealed; appellate result unverified
reports.status_qualification: Latest dated follow-up is an NGO statement announcing an expected 12 October 2022 ruling, not verification that the ruling occurred. Sources disagree on the December conviction and appeal dates. Amnesty describes a suspended custodial sentence; earlier sources describe provisional liberty. No current custody status is established.
executive: Unlike the June 2021 pre-disposition report, later sources establish a December 2021 conviction under Article 86 of the Telecommunications Code, a four-month custodial sentence and a TND 500 fine, followed by an appeal. Amnesty described the prison term as suspended and reported a prosecution appeal as well. The latest dated follow-up located, published on 9 October 2022, announced an expected ruling on 12 October; the ruling itself was not verified. [S2] [S4] [S5]

The proper conclusion is not acquittal, imprisonment served, or a final conviction. The subsequent appellate result and enforcement position remain unresolved in the researched record through 9 October 2026. The supplied report assigned no letter grade. [O]
baseline: Bribri, a blogger and activist documenting police abuses, faced proceedings over a Facebook video and accompanying criticism of police violence in October 2020. The original traced the complaint, questioning and successive hearing adjournments, with another hearing scheduled for 28 June 2021. At publication, it did not record a conviction. [O]

The report examined Article 86's prohibition of knowingly harming others or disturbing their peace through public telecommunications networks. Its concerns included the criminalization of political criticism, the breadth of the offense and effective preparation of the defense. These historical observations should not be silently converted into a judgment about the later appellate proceedings, whose records have not been obtained. [O]

timeline.event: Video and commentary on police violence led to the Article 86 prosecution.
Convicted and sentenced; HRW, the UN communication and Front Line Defenders give 21 December, while Amnesty gives 20 December.
Defense appeal filed; UN account gives 22 December and Amnesty 23 December. Amnesty also reports a prosecution appeal.
HRW reports provisional liberty pending appeal; historical custody observation only.
UN special rapporteurs send communication AL TUN 2/2022 concerning prosecution and defense safeguards.
Front Line Defenders announces an appeal session scheduled for 28 September in Sfax.
WJWC statement announces an expected 12 October ruling; no result established by this statement.

developments: HRW's January 2022 account, based in part on contact with Bribri, documented a conviction and provisional liberty pending appeal. The February UN communication likewise recorded an appeal and raised alleged restrictions on access to prosecution evidence. This was an actual communication by special rapporteurs to Tunisia, not merely a proposed submission, but it was not a judicial finding that Tunisia had violated a treaty. [S1] [S2]

Front Line Defenders' September notice confirms an announced appeal session. Amnesty's contemporaneous statement adds two legally important qualifications: it describes the sentence as suspended and says both defense and prosecution appealed. A suspended prison term is not imprisonment already served, and a prosecution appeal makes it unsafe to presume that only a reduction or acquittal was in issue. The exact procedural scope requires the appeal records. [S3] [S4]

The October WJWC statement supplies a later scheduled decision date, not the decision's contents. Searches under Myriam, Meriem, Breibri and Arabic spellings did not establish a certified or reliably reported appellate outcome. The absence of a located result is a research limitation, not evidence that the case had no later developments. [S5]
analysis: Analytical inference: the material change from the original is a movement from prosecution to conviction and appellate litigation. That materially changes the legal posture even though the outcome remains unverified. It is therefore inappropriate either to retain a simple 'awaiting trial' label or to infer finality from the passage of time. [O] [S2]

Analytical inference: the divergent dates and sentencing descriptions warrant preserving attribution rather than selecting one account without explanation. A registry extract or signed judgment could determine whether the apparent discrepancy concerns pronouncement, recording or reporting; none of those explanations is established here. [S1] [S4]
conclusion: A conviction and appeals are documented, but neither the scheduled appellate ruling nor subsequent enforcement has been verified. The follow-up should present that substantive development alongside an explicit unresolved-outcome qualification. [S2] [S4] [S5]
gaps: Signed first-instance judgment confirming date, suspension terms and fine.
Defense and prosecution appeal notices, their grounds and filing dates.
Whether a decision was delivered on 12 October 2022 or another date, and its operative terms.
Any later review, enforcement, payment or custody record, and Tunisia's response to AL TUN 2/2022.
